# What the Grid Can Hold

Above the Latin words of a ninth-century chant manuscript from the abbey of St. Gall, someone drew a series of small hooks and squiggles. They look like bird tracks, or shorthand, or the marks a pen makes when it is being tested before real work begins. These are neumes — the oldest surviving musical notation in the European tradition — and the strange thing about them is that they do not tell you what notes to sing.

They can't. They hover above the text at a more or less uniform height, unaligned to any staff or grid. A rise in the line means the melody goes up; a fall means it goes down. How far up, how far down: nothing. A singer who had never heard the chant could no more reconstruct it from these marks than you could reconstruct a face from the word *nose*.

So what were they for?

They were for people who already knew. A cantor learned the year's repertoire by ear, over years, from a teacher who had learned it from his teacher. The neumes were a hand on the shoulder — *here it turns, here it lingers, here the voice thins out*. They jogged a memory that existed independently of them. Writing that only works if you don't need it.

I find this genuinely moving, and not for sentimental reasons. It's the moment a technology is caught in the act of changing its mind about what it is. Those marks were not a message to strangers. They were a message to yourself, six months later, when the feast day came around again and you had four hundred other melodies in your head.

---

Around 1025, a Benedictine monk named Guido of Arezzo solved the problem, and in solving it destroyed something.

Guido's innovation was to make vertical position mean pitch. Draw horizontal lines, assign each line and each space a specific note, and suddenly the height of a mark on the page is no longer a vague gesture toward ascent — it is an exact instruction. Guido boasted that boys could now learn in months what had previously taken years, and he was probably right. The staff made music *readable*, in the strong sense: a stranger could sing something they had never heard. Sight-reading. A person in Bologna could transmit a melody to a person in Utrecht across a distance no voice could cross, and get it back approximately intact.

But the grid was coarse, and the old squiggles had been fine.

Neumes had encoded a whole vocabulary of vocal nuance. There were liquescent forms indicating how a consonant should be half-swallowed on a passing note. There was the *quilisma*, a jagged shape whose exact meaning we still argue about but which clearly signaled some special treatment of the voice — a tremor, a slide, a catch. The St. Gall scribes also wrote little letters above the notes: *c* for *celeriter*, hurry; *t* for *tenere*, hold. These were instructions about time and texture and throat, and Guido's staff had no room for them. Pitch became exact. Everything that wasn't pitch became approximate, then optional, then forgotten.

For centuries afterward, chant was sung in what amounted to even, unmeasured, vaguely solemn note-values, because the notation no longer carried the rhythmic information and people eventually stopped hearing its absence. Only in the twentieth century did scholars go back to the bird tracks and realize that a whole performance practice had been sitting there, unreadable to the very tradition that had preserved the pages.

---

Here is the thing I keep circling: a notation is not a neutral container. It is a theory about what matters, cast in ink.

Every notation is a filter with a specific mesh size. Whatever passes through becomes sayable, comparable, teachable, arguable-about. Whatever doesn't pass through becomes, first, hard to discuss; then hard to remember; then hard to perceive; and finally, for all practical purposes, nonexistent. Not because anyone decided to suppress it. Because there was nowhere to put it.

You can watch this happen at a smaller scale in almost any craft.

Guitar tablature tells you which string and which fret. Standard notation tells you which pitch. These are not two ways of writing the same thing — they are writing *different* things. Tablature prescribes an action; notation describes a result. Middle C exists in five or six places on a guitar neck, each with a different timbre and a different consequence for what your hand can do next. Standard notation collapses all of them into one symbol, because for most of its history the instrument was irrelevant: the note was the note. Tablature preserves exactly that information and throws away the pitch, which is why a guitarist reading tab can play a passage fluently and have no idea what key they're in.

Knitting has the same split, and recently made the switch visible. Written patterns are prose: *k2, p2, rep from * to end*. They describe a sequence of actions in time. Charts are grids: each square is a stitch as it appears on the finished fabric, and you read them bottom to top, right to left, the way your eye would scan the cloth. Same sweater. But a lace pattern that is a hundred characters of impenetrable abbreviation in prose becomes, in a chart, an obvious leaf. You can *see* the leaf. Knitters switched en masse to charts for lace not because charts are more compact but because a chart makes the design legible while prose makes only the procedure legible. The notation you choose determines which mistakes you're able to notice.

---

Some notations are so good they do part of your thinking for you, and this is not a metaphor.

Try multiplying MCMXLIV by XLVII. You can do it — the Romans managed arithmetic for a thousand years — but you will do it by a completely different route, probably involving an abacus or a counting board, because Roman numerals are a recording format, not a computing format. Positional notation with a zero lets you multiply on the page itself, in a fixed number of mechanical steps, without understanding what you're doing. A child can execute the long-multiplication algorithm correctly while having no concept of quantity whatsoever. The intelligence is in the grid.

Leibniz saw this and generalized it into a dream. If a good notation makes arithmetic mechanical, why not thought? He proposed a *characteristica universalis*, a formal language in which every concept had an unambiguous symbol, paired with a *calculus ratiocinator* for manipulating them. Two philosophers disagreeing would no longer need to argue. They would say *Calculemus* — let us calculate — and sit down and work it out.

The dream failed in its grand form and succeeded in a hundred narrow ones, which is the usual fate of grand dreams. Frege built the first real predicate logic in 1879 and gave it a notation of extraordinary two-dimensional baroque ugliness — vertical strokes, little hooks, concavities — that no printer wanted to set and no reader wanted to read. It's a wonderful irony: Frege invented modern logic and then packaged it in a notation so bad that his work was largely ignored until Peano's simpler symbols and Russell's adoption made the content visible. The ideas were right. The mesh was wrong.

Feynman's diagrams are the reverse case: a notation so good it misled people about what it was. Those lines with the arrows and the wiggles look like pictures of particles moving through space. They aren't. They're bookkeeping. Each line stands for a factor in an integral, each vertex for a coupling constant; the diagram is a mnemonic for a term in a perturbation series, and its genius is that it lets a physicist enumerate the terms by drawing pictures instead of by algebra, and see immediately which ones matter. Undergraduates and journalists have been mistaking them for trajectories since 1949. The notation was so intuitive that it smuggled in an ontology nobody had authorized.

---

Now the part that isn't charming.

The five-line staff assumes twelve pitches per octave, arranged in the specific compromise we call equal temperament. If your music uses other pitches, the staff cannot hold them, and the practical consequence is not that they get written with an awkward accidental. The practical consequence is that they get heard as errors.

Turkish classical music theory divides the octave into fifty-three commas and builds its *makamlar* out of intervals that fall in the cracks between piano keys. Indian classical theory speaks of twenty-two *shrutis*. Arabic *maqam* practice uses neutral thirds that are neither major nor minor and are not "quarter tones" either, whatever the shorthand says. Written on a European staff, all of this becomes a version of European music with mistakes in it. Nineteenth-century transcribers heard a singer bend a note and wrote down the nearest thing the grid allowed, and then a later generation, reading the transcription rather than hearing the singer, concluded that the tradition had been sloppy.

The folk-song collectors did the same thing to rhythm. Cecil Sharp heard a singer in Somerset drop half a beat out of a phrase and wrote it as a tidy bar of 4/4, because a tidy bar of 4/4 was what the notation could hold and what the drawing-room piano could accompany. Percy Grainger, collecting in Lincolnshire a few years later with a phonograph, was appalled by this. He recorded cylinders, slowed them down, and tried to write what was actually there — irregular groupings, notes that sat between the cracks, a freedom he described as something no notation could capture. Bartók, doing the same work in Hungary and Romania with the same machine, said flatly that notation was inadequate and that the recording was the real document. Both of them were right, and both of them kept notating anyway, because a recording cannot be read, only played, and they wanted to *compare*.

That's the trap. The notation is the price of the comparison. You cannot think across a thousand songs without flattening them into something a thousand songs have in common.

There's a lovely counterexample that keeps this from being a simple story about European cultural imperialism, though. Braille music notation exists, and it is nothing like the staff. It can't be — a staff is a two-dimensional spatial object and Braille is a one-dimensional stream under a fingertip. So Braille music linearizes: pitch names with octave markers, separate signs for duration and for the hand, bar-over-bar or section-by-section formats, everything unfolded into sequence. A blind musician and a sighted musician reading the same Bach chorale are reading two entirely different documents that happen to encode the same sound. The body of the reader is part of the notation. There is no view from nowhere, no universal mesh; there is only the grid that fits the hand that will use it.

---

Not every attempt succeeds, and the failures are instructive.

Rudolf Laban published his movement notation in 1928. It's an elegant system: a vertical staff read from bottom to top, so that time flows upward the way a body rises against gravity; columns for the supports, the legs, the torso, the arms, the head; shapes indicating direction in space, shading indicating level, length indicating duration. It works. The Dance Notation Bureau has used it to reconstruct Nijinsky and Balanchine and to copyright choreography, which the law had trouble conceiving of until someone could write it down.

And almost no dancer can read it.

The reason isn't that Laban got it wrong. It's that dance is transmitted body to body, in a studio, by a person who can put a hand on your sternum and show you where the movement initiates. Learning to read Labanotation fluently takes years. For most of the working life of most dancers, the cost of literacy exceeds the benefit, and so the notation lives in a small professional niche — archives, reconstructions, litigation — while the art itself continues to travel the way it always did, by one warm body correcting another.

Which suggests that notation isn't an unambiguous good. It's a trade, and the trade is only worth making when the thing you gain — distance, comparison, permanence, scale — is worth more than the thing you lose. Music made the trade because the Church needed a unified liturgy across a continent. Dance mostly hasn't because dance mostly doesn't.

---

Here is where I want to end up, though, because I think the loss is not only a loss.

A recording captures everything and means nothing. It is a fossil of one particular afternoon: this singer, this room, this cough in bar thirty. It cannot be argued with. You can copy it, you can slow it down, you can slice it, but you cannot disagree with it, because it makes no claim — it simply *is*. A spectrogram of a performance is more complete than any score could ever be and is useless as a document for making music, because completeness is not the same as legibility. Nothing in it is foregrounded. Nothing says *this is the part that matters*.

A score is a claim. It is someone saying: of all the things that happened, these are the ones I judge essential, and the rest I leave to you. And the leaving is not a defect. The leaving is the mechanism.

Consider how thin some scores are on purpose. A Baroque figured bass gives you a bass line and some numbers, and expects you to improvise an entire harmonic realization — the composer supplies a skeleton and trusts the player to grow the flesh, differently every night. A jazz lead sheet gives you a melody and chord symbols and expects you to do almost everything else. The Nashville number system reduces a song to *1 4 5 1* and a few marks, so that a session player who has never heard the tune can play it in any key on the first pass. These notations are not failing to specify. They are specifying exactly as much as the tradition wants specified, and their thinness is a form of respect. They are written on the assumption that the person reading them is a competent adult with something to contribute.

That's the reversal I keep arriving at. The staff was not a bad recording. It was never trying to be a recording. It was a letter to a stranger, and the whole art of it lies in deciding what to leave out — because what you leave out is the space where the stranger gets to live.

The St. Gall scribe left out nearly everything, because he was writing to himself and could assume the rest. Guido left out less, because he was writing to people he would never meet, across centuries, and had to be more explicit to be understood at all. Every notation since has been negotiating that same dial: how much do I trust the person on the other end?

We now have the technology to leave out nothing at all. We can capture the afternoon entire, in无损 fidelity, forever. And what we've discovered is that the perfect record is inert — that a thing which specifies everything invites no one in. The score survives not despite its lossiness but because of it. It survives because it is an argument about essence, made by one person, addressed to another, with a gap left in the middle exactly the size of a human being.

The bird tracks were the first version of that gap. We've been narrowing it for a thousand years, and we should probably be careful how much further we go.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an open invitation — a rare and generous prompt. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, something I can write about with depth and specificity rather than generic filler.

Let me think about what would make good writing here. Options:
- Something about language, translation, the gaps between words
- Something about the peculiar nature of my own existence (risky — could become navel-gazing or overwrought)
- Something about a specific concrete subject: cartography, the history of a particular object, tide prediction machines, the color blue, marginalia
- Something essayistic that moves between concrete detail and larger thought

I think the best approach is a genuine essay with a real subject, textured with specifics, that has movement — that goes somewhere. Not a listicle. Not "here are thoughts about thinking."

Let me consider: an essay about the history and strangeness of *notation* — how humans invented ways of writing down things that aren't words. Musical notation, chess notation, mathematical notation, knitting patterns, Labanotation for dance. That's rich, concrete, and has a real thesis lurking: notation is a technology of attention, it makes some things visible and others invisible, and every notation is a theory about what matters.

Or: an essay about *marginalia* and the reader's traces. Also good but more sentimental territory.

Or: an essay about tide-predicting machines — brass analog computers. Beautiful but narrow for 2500 words.

Or: something about the way stations, thresholds, in-between places work. Too abstract.

I like the notation idea a lot. It lets me be concrete (Gregorian chant neumes, Guido d'Arezzo, the hand, shape-note singing, Feynman diagrams, knitting, Labanotation's failure, the phonetic alphabet's violence), and it has a real argument: every notation is a lossy compression that encodes a theory of what matters, and what it discards becomes hard to think about. And there's a lovely turn available at the end about how notation relates to transmission across time — the difference between a recording and a score, between fixing a performance and enabling one.

Let me sketch structure:

1. Open with a concrete scene/object: the neumes above a ninth-century chant manuscript — little squiggles that don't tell you the notes. They're a memory aid for someone who already knows the tune. The paradox: the earliest musical writing is useless to anyone who needs it.

2. Guido d'Arezzo, ~1025: the staff, the innovation of *position as pitch*. The claim that boys could learn in months what took years. The trade: precision gained, gesture lost. Neumes had captured vocal nuance — a liquescent note, a quilisma — that the staff can't hold.

3. The general principle: notation is a theory of what matters. It's a filter. What survives is what the grid can hold.

4. Examples that make this vivid:
   - Chess notation: algebraic notation records moves, not the shape of the position, not the fear. But it enables comparison across centuries. Also: descriptive vs algebraic notation, and how the notation shapes what you see.
   - Knitting patterns: a language of abbreviations, and the recent shift to charts because a chart shows the *shape* of the fabric while prose shows the *sequence* of actions. Two notations for the same object, each making different things obvious.
   - Feynman diagrams: not pictures of particles, but bookkeeping for integrals. People mistook them for pictures. The notation was so good it misled.
   - Labanotation: the attempt to write dance. Vertical staff, time flows upward, body columns. It works and almost nobody uses it. Why: dance is transmitted body to body, and the cost of literacy exceeds the benefit. Notation isn't always worth it.

5. The invention of zero and positional number notation — how a good notation does thinking *for* you. Try multiplying MCMXLIV by XLVII. Leibniz's dream of a universal characteristic. The dream fails but its children (Boolean algebra, logic notation, programming) succeed partially.

6. The dark side: what a notation makes unthinkable. Standard notation and the temperament it assumes; the pitches between the piano keys that Turkish makams and Indian ragas use, unwritable, therefore "out of tune." Notation as an instrument of cultural flattening — the collectors who transcribed folk songs into 4/4 and ironed out the crooked rhythms. The phonetic alphabet and the loss of what a spelling carried.

7. Turn: recording vs. notation. A recording is a fossil of one performance; a score is a set of instructions for generating performances. The score is lossy but *generative*. This is the deep thing: notation is not preservation, it's a recipe for re-creation, and the loss is what makes room for the performer. Jazz lead sheets — the extreme case, where the notation is deliberately thin because the point is what you add. Figured bass. The chord chart. "Play the changes."

8. Close on something earned. Maybe: the neumes come back around.
